_comment: Per-country connectivity facts for /tools/esim pages. English source of truth; prose fields (intro, coverage, tips) are translated by scripts/translate-esim.mjs into src/i18n/esim-i18n.json with a srcHash stamp, so editing a field here re-queues its translations. EVERGREEN FACTS ONLY: carrier names and coverage character — never prices, plan sizes or vendor claims (those go stale and we link to live pricing instead). Keyed by countries.json slug; a country gets an eSIM page when it is active in countries.json AND has an entry here.

japan.name: Japan
japan.intro: Japan runs on four nationwide networks — NTT Docomo, au (KDDI), SoftBank and the newer Rakuten Mobile. Travel eSIMs almost always ride one of the big three, and for a visitor the practical difference between them is small: all three are fast and dependable in the places tourists actually go.
japan.coverage: City coverage is superb, and unusually for the world, that includes the underground — you keep a signal on Tokyo and Osaka metro platforms and inside most trains. Coverage follows the shinkansen lines well. Where it thins out is deep in the mountains: remote onsen valleys, high hiking trails and some stretches of rural Hokkaido can drop to weak or no signal, so download offline maps before a countryside day trip.
tips: Japan is still surprisingly cash-based, but it is also map-app-dependent: addresses are hard to navigate without data, so a working connection matters more here than in most countries.
Free WiFi exists in convenience stores, hotels and many stations, but it is patchy and login-walled on the street — plan on mobile data rather than hopping between hotspots.
Train-planning apps (route search, platform numbers, delays) are the single biggest data use for visitors — make sure your plan has enough data for heavy map and transit use.
Airport SIM counters and vending machines exist at the major airports, but after a long-haul landing the queue and the paperwork are exactly what an eSIM installed at home lets you skip.

thailand.name: Thailand
thailand.intro: Thailand's mobile market is dominated by two big networks: AIS, the largest, and True, which absorbed dtac in their 2023 merger. Most travel eSIMs connect through one of these two, and both are strong in every place on a normal tourist route.
thailand.coverage: Bangkok, Chiang Mai and the coastal cities have fast, dense coverage, and the popular islands — Phuket, Samui, Phangan, Krabi's beaches — are well served in towns and resort areas. Signal gets patchy on remote beaches, in national parks and in the mountainous border regions, so treat a jungle trek or a far-flung island cove as offline time.
tips: Daily life for a visitor runs on data: Grab for rides, translation apps at street stalls, and QR codes everywhere — Thailand is one of the most QR-payment-heavy countries you will visit.

Tourist SIM counters at Suvarnabhumi and Don Mueang airports are famous and genuinely fine — but they meet every long-haul arrival wave, so an eSIM installed before departure saves you the one queue you least want after a red-eye.
Island-hopping? Coverage is best in populated areas; boats between islands and quiet stretches of coast can be dead zones, so download tickets and maps before you leave WiFi.
If your trip includes long bus or train legs (Bangkok–Chiang Mai, the southern lines), coverage along the routes is decent but variable — download entertainment in advance.

south-korea.name: South Korea
south-korea.intro: South Korea's three networks — SK Telecom, KT and LG U+ — run some of the fastest, densest mobile infrastructure anywhere. Travel eSIMs ride one of the three, and for a visitor there is no bad pick: all three are excellent everywhere tourists go.
south-korea.coverage: Coverage is close to total: full signal in the Seoul and Busan subways, in KTX trains at 300 km/h, in mountain national parks and on Jeju's coastal roads. It is genuinely hard to find a dead zone on a normal itinerary — the practical question in Korea is not whether you will have signal, but how much data you will burn.
tips: Google Maps barely works for navigation in Korea — locals and visitors alike use Naver Map or Kakao Map, both data-hungry and both essential from day one.
Taxis run on Kakao T and payments lean on apps and QR — a working connection replaces a lot of pointing and guessing.
Free WiFi is common in cafés and subways, but juggling logins is friction you don't need in a country this connected — mobile data is the smooth path.
Incheon airport's SIM counters are efficient but meet every arrival wave; an eSIM installed before departure means you walk straight past them.

vietnam.name: Vietnam
vietnam.intro: Vietnam has three main networks — Viettel, Vinaphone and MobiFone. Viettel, run with military-grade ambition, is the largest and has the strongest rural footprint; the other two are solid in cities and towns. Which network a travel eSIM uses matters more here than in most countries, precisely because of that rural gap.
vietnam.coverage: Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, Da Nang and every provincial city are well covered with fast data. The differences show up in the mountains and the countryside: the Ha Giang loop, Sapa's valleys and remote stretches of the central highlands are where Viettel keeps a bar or two while others fade. On the classic north–south route the populated corridor is fine on any network.
tips: Grab (rides) and a translation app are near-essential in Vietnam, and both are useless without data — get connected before you need your first ride from the airport.
Doing the Ha Giang loop, Sapa treks or other mountain riding? Prefer a plan on Viettel's network and still expect dead zones on the passes — download offline maps.
Buying a physical SIM locally means passport registration at the counter; an eSIM bought before the trip skips the paperwork entirely.
Hotel and café WiFi is everywhere and genuinely fast in cities — your data plan mostly needs to cover the hours in between, so mid-sized plans go further than you might expect.

united-states.name: United States
united-states.intro: The US has three nationwide networks — AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon. Most travel eSIMs connect through T-Mobile or AT&T; Verizon rarely appears in travel plans. In cities and suburbs all three are fast and dependable.
united-states.coverage: Coverage maps and reality agree in metro areas and along interstates, then diverge in the rural West: national parks, desert stretches and mountain roads can go dark for long spells on any network. If your trip is a road trip, treat connectivity as a city amenity and plan the empty stretches offline.
tips: Distances are the trap: a two-week road trip burns far more navigation data than a two-week city trip, and the places you need maps most are the places with the least signal — download offline maps for every park and desert leg.
Free WiFi is genuinely everywhere in chains, hotels and malls, which takes pressure off your data plan in cities.
If your route leans rural, check which US network the eSIM uses before buying — the T-Mobile/AT&T difference matters more out there than any price gap.
Ride-hailing, mobile boarding passes and parking apps make the US surprisingly data-dependent for a country this WiFi-rich — keep data working on travel days especially.

france.name: France
france.intro: France has four national networks — Orange, SFR, Bouygues Telecom and Free Mobile — and travel eSIMs ride one of them. Because France is in the EU roaming zone, many eSIMs sold for France actually cover all of Europe, which changes how you should shop.
france.coverage: Paris and every major city are solidly covered, including most of the Paris métro. Coverage stays good along the TGV lines and in towns; it thins in deep countryside — wine-country back roads, Alpine valleys and some village interiors with thick stone walls where indoor signal drops.
tips: Crossing borders? Buy a Europe-wide eSIM rather than a France-only one — one plan covers a Paris–Rome–Barcelona trip under EU roaming rules.
Train travel runs on the SNCF Connect app — tickets, platforms and strike updates all want data at exactly the moment station WiFi is weakest.
Download offline maps for villages and wine regions; the prettiest detours are the least covered.
Café WiFi exists but is nobody's plan A in France — mobile data is the reliable path, and city coverage makes it painless.

italy.name: Italy
italy.intro: Italy's four networks — TIM, Vodafone, WindTre and Iliad — all serve travel eSIMs, and Italy sits in the EU roaming zone, so Europe-wide plans cover it too. In the cities and along the coast, any of them will do fine.
italy.coverage: Rome, Milan, Florence and Venice are well covered outdoors; the classic Italian surprise is indoors, where metre-thick historic walls can smother a signal in the very buildings you came to see. Rural Tuscany, the deep south and Alpine valleys are patchier than the tourist cities.
tips: Doing Italy as part of a wider European trip? A Europe-wide eSIM is usually the smarter buy than an Italy-only plan.
Train apps (Trenitalia, Italo) handle tickets and platform changes — have data working before you're running for a regionale.
Hill towns, the Amalfi coast's cliff roads and the Dolomites all have dead spots — download offline maps before day trips.
If your accommodation is a centro storico building, expect weak indoor signal on any network — it's the walls, not your plan.

china.name: China
china.intro: China's three networks — China Mobile, China Unicom and China Telecom — have vast, fast coverage. The real question for visitors is not signal but access: local networks operate under China's internet rules, so many familiar apps behave differently there. Travel eSIMs that connect as international roaming route data through the provider's home network, which is why many travelers find their usual apps keep working on them — always check what the specific provider says it supports before relying on it.
china.coverage: City coverage is excellent, including metros and high-speed rail lines. Coverage reaches remarkably far into the countryside by any international standard, though remote mountain and western regions still thin out.
tips: Payments are the big one: daily life runs on Alipay and WeChat Pay, both of which accept foreign cards — set them up before you fly, and remember both need a working connection at every checkout.
Navigation: Amap (Gaode) and Baidu Maps are what actually knows every alley; they want data constantly.
Confirm with your eSIM provider which apps and services work on their China plans — providers state this explicitly, and it varies. Don't discover the answer at the airport.
Hotel WiFi follows the same local rules as local networks — a roaming eSIM and hotel WiFi can behave differently on the same phone, which is normal, not a malfunction.

spain.name: Spain
spain.intro: Spain's main networks — Movistar, Vodafone and Orange — cover the mainland and both archipelagos well, and Spain is in the EU roaming zone, so Europe-wide eSIMs work here including the Balearics and Canaries.
spain.coverage: Madrid, Barcelona and the coastal cities have dense, fast coverage; the islands are well served in populated areas. Signal thins in the emptier interior — rural Extremadura, mountain stretches of Andalucía and the Pyrenees — and, as in Italy, thick old-town walls can weaken indoor reception.
tips: Island-bound? Confirm the plan covers Spain's islands — EU-wide and Spain plans do, but it's worth the ten-second check for the Canaries.
Renfe tickets, metro apps and restaurant bookings all live on your phone here — Spain is more app-driven than its laid-back reputation suggests.
Multi-country Iberia trips (Portugal, Morocco day-trips aside) fit a Europe-wide plan better than a Spain-only one — note Morocco is NOT in the EU zone.
Download offline maps for white-village driving routes and the Camino stretches — the gaps are exactly where the scenery peaks.

united-arab-emirates.name: United Arab Emirates
united-arab-emirates.intro: The UAE has two networks — e& (formerly Etisalat) and du — and both are superb: dense 5G in Dubai and Abu Dhabi, strong signal in malls, metros and even most of the desert highways.
united-arab-emirates.coverage: Coverage is effectively total in the cities and along the intercity corridors. The practical quirk of the UAE is regulatory, not technical: internet calling (WhatsApp, FaceTime and similar voice/video calls) is restricted in the country on any network, so messaging works normally while calls often do not.
tips: Plan around the VoIP restriction: WhatsApp texts flow normally, but voice and video calls over the usual apps are blocked on local networks — some travelers find roaming eSIMs behave differently, but never promise a client call from Dubai on WhatsApp.
Careem (the local Uber) and the metro's nol app want data; taxis are card-friendly but hailing by app beats hailing by hand in the heat.
Coverage is so good that a small-data plan often suffices — malls and hotels shower you with fast WiFi.

If a working phone number matters for your trip, this is one country where a local physical SIM (sold at the airport with your passport) still has an edge — data-only eSIMs can't receive the SMS codes some UAE services send.

taiwan.name: Taiwan
taiwan.intro: Taiwan's three networks — Chunghwa Telecom, Taiwan Mobile and FarEasTone — are all strong, with Chunghwa holding the widest-coverage reputation. Travel eSIMs are plentiful and the island's compact geography makes any of the three a fine choice for the standard loop.
taiwan.coverage: Taipei, the west-coast cities and the high-speed rail corridor are blanketed, metro included. The east coast (Hualien, Taitung) is well covered in towns; the central mountains — Taroko's gorges, alpine highway passes, Yushan trails — are where signal drops on every network.
tips: Taoyuan airport's telecom counters are famously quick and tourist-friendly — but they still queue at peak arrival hours, which is the one line an eSIM installed at home deletes from your trip.
Night-market hopping and bus routes run on data: Google Maps works well here, and YouBike rental needs a connection to unlock.
Heading into Taroko or up the alpine roads? Download offline maps — the gorge walls block signal in exactly the most photogenic spots.
Convenience-store WiFi exists but registration is clunky for visitors — data is the smooth path, and Taiwan's plans are famously generous.

indonesia.name: Indonesia
indonesia.intro: Indonesia's big three are Telkomsel, XL Axiata and Indosat — and which one your eSIM uses matters more here than almost anywhere, because Telkomsel's coverage lead grows the further you get from Java and Bali.
indonesia.coverage: Jakarta, Bali's south and the main Javanese cities are well covered. Beyond them the archipelago spreads thin: Nusa Penida's cliff sides, Komodo boat routes, rural Lombok and anywhere in eastern Indonesia can drop to nothing — Telkomsel keeps signal longest, which is why locals in remote areas carry it.
tips: Going beyond Bali and Java? Prefer a plan that rides Telkomsel's network — on the outer islands the difference is not speed, it's signal versus none.
Grab and Gojek are how you move and eat — get data working before you leave the airport, because ordering the first ride is when you need it most.
Indonesia registers phone IMEIs for locally bought SIMs on longer stays; a travel eSIM connecting as roaming sidesteps that paperwork entirely for a normal holiday.
Boat days (island hopping, Komodo, surf trips) are offline days — download maps, tickets and entertainment the night before.

malaysia.name: Malaysia
malaysia.intro: Malaysia's networks — Maxis, CelcomDigi (merged in 2022) and U Mobile — give strong, cheap connectivity across the peninsula. Travel eSIMs typically ride Maxis or CelcomDigi, and in Kuala Lumpur, Penang and Melaka you will not tell them apart.
malaysia.coverage: The west-coast corridor is densely covered; the peninsula's interior (Cameron Highlands' winding roads, Taman Negara's jungle) gets patchy. East Malaysia — Sabah and Sarawak on Borneo — is fine in Kota Kinabalu and Kuching but drops fast in the interior and on dive trips.
tips: Grab is the default for rides and food across Malaysia — the airport-to-city Grab is your first data moment.
Heading to Borneo? Coverage assumptions from KL do not transfer — treat jungle lodges, dive boats and mountain treks as offline and download accordingly.
KLIA's SIM counters are cheap and competent, but arrivals bunch up — the eSIM-at-home move saves the queue after an overnight flight.
Malls and cafés hand out WiFi freely in the cities, so your data mostly needs to cover transit and street time — mid-sized plans stretch well here.

india.name: India
india.intro: India runs on three networks — Reliance Jio, Airtel and Vi — with Jio and Airtel far ahead on coverage and speed. Buying a local SIM as a foreigner means passport paperwork and a wait for activation, which is exactly the friction a travel eSIM bought before the trip removes.
india.coverage: Cities and towns are strongly covered by Jio and Airtel, and the rail corridors between them mostly hold signal. Remote Himalayan valleys (Ladakh, Spiti), desert stretches of Rajasthan and tribal-belt interiors thin out on every network — and in a few sensitive border regions, connectivity is restricted for everyone.
tips: Prefer plans riding Jio or Airtel — Vi's coverage gap is real once you leave the metros.

Ubers/Olas, train-status apps and QR payments make urban India intensely data-driven — but note most UPI QR payments need an Indian bank account, so carry a card backup and use data for maps and rides.
Long train journeys are part of the experience: download offline maps and entertainment, and expect signal to come and go with the towns.

A data-only eSIM cannot receive Indian SMS codes; if a service insists on an Indian number, that is a counter-with-passport errand — for a normal tourist itinerary, WhatsApp on your home number covers everything.

philippines.name: Philippines
philippines.intro: The Philippines is a two-network country — Globe and Smart — spread across 7,000 islands. Both are solid in Manila, Cebu and the major tourist hubs; across the archipelago their strongholds alternate, so neither wins everywhere.
philippines.coverage: Metro Manila, Cebu City, Boracay, El Nido town and Siargao's main strip are all workable. Between islands and away from town centers, coverage drops quickly: ferry crossings, remote beaches and inland barangays can be dead air, and storms genuinely take towers down for days.
tips: Island-hopping days are offline days: boats, sandbars and lagoons have no signal — screenshot bookings and download maps the night before.
The Philippines registers local SIM buyers by law; a travel eSIM roaming in sidesteps the registration queue at the airport.
Grab works in the big cities; elsewhere it's tricycles and habal-habal negotiated in person — data matters most in cities and least on the islands you came for.
During typhoon season, mobile networks are your storm-warning channel — keep some data in reserve and charge a power bank when weather turns.

turkey.name: Turkey
turkey.intro: Turkey's three networks — Turkcell, Vodafone and Türk Telekom — cover the tourist map well, with Turkcell holding the strongest overall reputation. Turkey is not in the EU roaming zone, so a Europe eSIM that carried you through Greece stops paying its way at the border — check for Turkey by name.
turkey.coverage: Istanbul, the Aegean and Mediterranean coasts and Cappadocia's hotel towns are well covered. Central Anatolia's steppe, the east and mountain roads run patchier; underground cisterns, hammams and the Grand Bazaar's vaulted lanes can smother indoor signal.
tips: Buying a Europe-wide plan? Confirm it lists Turkey explicitly — many EU-zone plans do not include it, and finding out at Istanbul Airport is the expensive way.
Turkey registers the IMEI of foreign phones that use local SIMs beyond a grace period; a short-stay roaming eSIM never touches that system.
Istanbul runs on apps — BiTaksi for cabs, ferry timetables, Istanbulkart top-ups — and the city's scale makes offline improvisation genuinely hard.
Hot-air-balloon mornings in Cappadocia start with 4 a.m. pickup confirmations by WhatsApp — have data working the night before, not after landing.

singapore.name: Singapore
singapore.intro: Singapore's three networks — Singtel, StarHub and M1 — blanket one of the world's most connected cities. Every travel eSIM works well here; there is no coverage strategy to think about, only how much data you want.
singapore.coverage: Coverage is total: full-speed signal in the MRT tunnels, in basements of malls, on Sentosa's beaches and across the entire island. Singapore is the rare destination where the coverage section of this guide has nothing to warn you about.
tips: Small plans go far: the city is dense, distances are short, and free WiFi saturates malls, hotels and the airport — you mostly need data in transit.
Grab, MRT maps and hawker-centre queues via Google Maps are the daily data uses; nothing here is data-heavy.
Changi sells SIMs efficiently on arrival, but an eSIM means you exit straight to the Jewel waterfall instead of a counter.
Using Singapore as a hub? Consider a regional Asia eSIM covering Singapore + Malaysia + Indonesia in one plan for multi-stop trips.
